strengths: A well-motivated and elegant framework (DLL) that turns deterministic neural operators into conditional generative models by combining an input-dependent operator encoder with a latent diffusion model.

Strong theoretical foundation with proofs establishing that the operator encoder learns an optimal rank-r truncated Karhunen-Loève (KL) expansion, and linking the diffusion velocity-matching loss directly to Wasserstein distance stability bounds.

Excellent experimental results on both stochastic operator learning (stochastic Burgers, Darcy flow) and chaotic autoregressive rollouts (Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, Kolmogorov flow), demonstrating superior calibration, accuracy, and rollout stability.
Highly clear presentation with excellent illustrative figures (e.g., Figures 1 & 2) and comprehensive, detailed appendices containing both proofs and architectural parameters.
weaknesses: The paper lacks an ablation study on the key hyperparameter, the latent dimension r. It would be highly informative to see how the reconstruction quality and generative fidelity scale with r.

Comparison with other native function-space generative models (such as functional flow matching or infinite-dimensional diffusion models) is missing. Since discretization invariance is a core motivation for neural operators, comparing only against grid-bound diffusion models (DM, LDM) on regular grids slightly limits the evaluation of this aspect.

There is a lack of quantitative timing and computational overhead benchmarks (e.g., training time, sampling wall-clock time) comparing DLL against DM and LDM in the main text to fully support the 'lightweight' and 'efficient' claims.

strengths: Elegant and Practical Methodology: Combining neural operators with latent diffusion by training the diffusion model directly on the coefficients of an input-dependent basis is a clever and highly practical approach. It preserves discretization invariance while significantly reducing the computational overhead of diffusion sampling.

Rigorous Theoretical Analysis: The paper provides strong theoretical foundations. Proposition 4.1 establishes that the learned operator encoder approximates the optimal rank-r Karhunen-Loève expansion of the conditional distribution. The Wasserstein stability estimates in Proposition 2.3 and Appendix A mathematically connect the velocity matching loss to distribution approximation.

Strong Empirical Performance: The proposed DLL is comprehensively evaluated across both stochastic (Burgers, Darcy) and chaotic/deterministic (Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, Kolmogorov flow) systems. It demonstrates excellent calibration (as measured by the spread-to-skill ratio) and rollout stability, often outperforming much larger pixel-space or latent diffusion models with fewer parameters.

Excellent Clarity and Presentation: The paper is exceptionally well-structured, written, and visualized. The training and inference pipeline is clearly illustrated, and the qualitative results in the appendix are very informative.
weaknesses: Lack of Empirical Comparison to Function-Space Diffusion Models: While the authors compare to standard discretized latent diffusion models (LDM) and pixel-space diffusion (DM), they omit empirical comparisons to infinite-dimensional or function-space diffusion/flow matching models. Even on regular grids, these models would serve as important baselines to highlight the efficiency and accuracy of DLL's low-rank formulation.

Missing Ablation on Latent Dimension r: The choice of r = 64 is kept constant across all benchmarks. An ablation study showing the sensitivity of both reconstruction error and generative performance to different values of the latent rank r is missing, which would help clarify the limits of the low-rank assumption.

Two-Stage Training Limitation: The model requires a two-stage training procedure (first training and freezing the operator encoder, then training the diffusion head). A discussion on whether end-to-end training is feasible or why the two-stage process is strictly preferred would have provided more practical insights.

strengths: The paper is exceptionally well-written, with clear explanations, illustrative figures, and a precise mathematical formulation of the probabilistic operator learning framework.

The theoretical foundation is solid: the authors provide rigorous proofs showing that the operator encoder design mathematically recovers the optimal conditional Karhunen-Loève expansion, and they provide Wasserstein stability estimates for the conditional diffusion process.

The input-dependent basis design (Φ(a)) is highly elegant and effective. By conditioning the basis on the input, the model achieves much higher reconstruction accuracy at lower latent dimensions compared to standard autoencoders, as demonstrated in Tables 6 and 7.

Strong empirical results across both stochastic PDE benchmarks and chaotic autoregressive rollouts. DLL exhibits excellent uncertainty calibration (indicated by the spread-to-skill ratio) and outperforms grid-based diffusion baselines while being significantly more parameter-efficient.
weaknesses: While neural operators are fundamentally valued for their discretization-invariant (or resolution-independent) properties, the paper lacks empirical verification of zero-shot super-resolution. It is critical to show whether the diffusion process trained on one resolution can successfully generate high-fidelity samples at a higher resolution without retraining.

The proposed framework relies on a multi-stage training pipeline (first training the operator encoder, freezing it, and then training the diffusion last layer). An end-to-end joint training alternative is not explored or discussed, which could potentially simplify the optimization workflow.

The performance of the Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) baseline is remarkably poor on several tasks (e.g., Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and Kolmogorov rollouts in Tables 4 and 5). A deeper analysis or discussion is needed to explain why the standard LDM fails so severely compared to DLL in preserving fine-scale physical structures.

strengths: A well-motivated and elegant framework (DLL) that successfully bridges generative diffusion models and neural operators by learning a conditional diffusion model over input-dependent low-rank coefficients.

Strong theoretical support, including the connection of the operator encoder to the optimal rank-r conditional uncentered Karhunen-Loève subspace (Proposition 4.1) and stability guarantees for the conditional generative process.

Comprehensive empirical evaluations across both stochastic PDEs (aleatoric uncertainty) and chaotic rollouts (epistemic/compounding uncertainty), demonstrating superior or competitive performance against strong baselines.
Excellent ablation studies analyzing critical factors such as latent rank, number of function evaluations (NFE), training dataset size, and compatibility with different architectures (DeepONet).
weaknesses: The training pipeline is decoupled into two stages (first training the operator encoder, then freezing it to train the diffusion head). It is unclear if joint end-to-end training is feasible or if it would improve the performance.

The representation capability is ultimately bounded by the low-rank assumption. As seen in the Kolmogorov flow results (Table 5), pixel-space diffusion (DM) still outperforms DLL on complex 2D chaotic dynamics in terms of NRMSE and CRPS.

While sampling in coefficient space is faster than in pixel space, the multi-step ODE integration still incurs significantly more inference overhead compared to single-forward probabilistic operators like PNO. An explicit runtime comparison would help clarify this trade-off.

strengths: The proposed Diffusion Last Layer (DLL) is a highly elegant and modular framework that successfully bridges neural operators and conditional generative models to perform uncertainty quantification.

Strong theoretical support is provided: the paper successfully relates the learned operator encoder to the optimal rank-r uncentered Karhunen-Loève expansion, and provides stability bounds in Wasserstein distance for the conditional diffusion velocity matching objective.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation across diverse 1D and 2D benchmarks (both stochastic SPDEs and deterministic chaotic rollouts) demonstrating strong performance against competitive baselines (like PNO, pixel-space, and latent-space diffusion models).
Excellent parameter and computational efficiency: by performing diffusion in a low-dimensional coefficient space rather than pixel-space, DLL drastically reduces the cost of conditional generation.
The manuscript is outstandingly well-written, clear, and includes extensive ablation studies and qualitative results in the appendix.
weaknesses: As noted by the authors, DLL's performance ceiling is heavily dependent on the expressive power of the underlying deterministic neural operator backbone, which sometimes places it slightly behind pixel-space diffusion (DM) in complex settings like the Kolmogorov flow.

The operator encoder's reconstruction error, while small, shows some non-monotonicity or performance trade-offs in highly stochastic scenarios compared to standard grid-based autoencoders (as shown in Tables 6 and 7).
Finding the optimal rank $r$ is non-trivial and requires empirical tuning, as downstream metrics are not always monotonic with respect to the latent dimension.

strengths: The paper presents a well-formulated and elegant framework (Diffusion Last Layer) that integrates neural operators with conditional diffusion/flow matching in an input-dependent low-rank coefficient space.
The theoretical grounding is a key strength, establishing formal connections to the uncentered Karhunen–Loève expansion (Proposition 4.1) and providing Wasserstein stability bounds (Proposition 2.3).
The method successfully preserves discretization invariance and operator learning structure, avoiding grid-bound discrete autoencoders typical in standard latent diffusion models.

The empirical evaluation is comprehensive, covering both intrinsically stochastic problems (Burgers, Darcy) and chaotic deterministic rollouts (KS, Kolmogorov), accompanied by thorough ablation studies (rank, NFE, backbone compatibility).
weaknesses: Performance on complex 2D systems is somewhat limited; on Kolmogorov flow (Table 5), the grid-based pixel-space diffusion baseline (DM) significantly outperforms the proposed DLL in both NRMSE and CRPS, showing that standard spatial inductive biases can still dominate.

The training pipeline is decoupled into two stages (first training the operator encoder, freezing it, and then training the MLP-based diffusion head), which may lead to sub-optimal representations compared to joint, end-to-end optimization.

The parameter count for the 2D operator encoder (OE) is quite large (17.94M parameters as shown in Table 9), which is nearly double that of the LDM autoencoder baseline (9.74M), raising some concerns about memory efficiency on higher-dimensional tasks.

The paper lacks direct empirical comparisons against other infinite-dimensional or function-space diffusion models (e.g., Functional Flow Matching or score-based models in Hilbert spaces), which also offer discretization-robust generative capabilities.
